learningObjective: Distinguish sound and precise analyses and identify the direction of over-/under-approximation.

canonicalClaims.claim: Soundness of a static analysis is defined relative to intent: for compiler optimizations it is a may-analysis (over-approximation) so no illegal transformation is enabled; for bug-finding it may be an under-approximation (only true bugs reported). Precision is a separate axis measuring closeness to the ideal answer.
conditions: Analysis is defined within an abstract interpretation or dataflow framework.
Sound direction is stated with respect to the intended use (transformation legality vs bug reporting).
nonImplications: Does not imply sound analyses are precise.
Does not imply unsound analyses are useless in practice; heuristic tools are widely used.

misconceptions.claim: A sound analysis is always precise.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The trivially conservative analysis (e.g., 'may-alias with everything') is sound but has zero precision. Soundness and precision are orthogonal.
Direction depends on intent. For optimization analyses, soundness means over-approximation (no false 'safe' answers); for bug-finding, soundness may mean no false positives.

misconceptions.claim: All static analyses in production compilers are provably sound.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Many practical analyses (especially in linters and JITs) trade soundness for scalability or usability; some are known-unsound and still useful.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: Livshits et al., 'In Defense of Soundiness'

implementationFacts: Sound under-approximation (bug-finding): must-alias, must-happen, definite null.
performanceScenarios: Optimizer must use sound may-analyses to preserve correctness; increasing precision typically shrinks conservative fallbacks and enables more optimizations.
